explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The LORD says to Joshua, “…as I instructed you through Moses…” Moses was Israel's leader, so these instructions were already on the books. I hear a thing once and call it done, then lose it before the cookies cool.

Aaron was Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), so I see how he got in the mix. But the LORD names Moses here: “…as I instructed you through Moses…” The text doesn't say Aaron in this verse. Keep the brothers straight, friend, and you're golden.

Samuel was a prophet in Israel (1 Samuel 3:20), but he doesn't show up in this passage. The LORD says the instructions came “through Moses.” Moses, Israel's leader, is the name to grab. Nice try, friend, and a good name to know anyway.

explanations.answer: Someone who kills another by accident
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. God says these cities are so that “…anyone who kills another unintentionally or accidentally may flee there.” That's who the refuge is for. An accident is no small thing, and God made a place for it.

explanations.answer: Someone who steals from a neighbor
explanations.explanation: Stealing isn't what God names here. The verse is about someone who kills another “…unintentionally or accidentally…” That's the one who may flee to these cities. I once stamped a whole batch with the apron on backwards, so I know about small mix-ups. This isn't one of them, friend.

Breaking a promise isn't in this verse, friend. God says the one who may flee is someone who kills another “…unintentionally or accidentally…” The refuge is from the avenger of blood. So the verse stays on an accidental killing, and that's where we stay too.

Right on the money, friend. The one who flees “…states his case before its elders…” Then the elders bring him into the city and give him a place to live among them. They're the ones listening at the gate.

Priests are close, since the high priest does come up later in verse 6. But at the gate, the text says the man states his case before the city's elders. The elders bring him in and give him a place to live. Good guess, friend, but the elders are the ones at this gate.

That sounds like a fine job title, friend. But the text says nothing about gatekeepers here. The one who flees stands at the entrance of the gate and states his case before the city's elders. Then they bring him in.
Not quite, friend. The text says the elders “…are to bring him into the city and give him a place to live among them.” He isn't left outside the walls. They take him in and give him a place to stay.

Correct, it's false. Here's what God says: the elders “…are to bring him into the city and give him a place to live among them.” Nobody sends him out to camp by the wall. He gets a place inside, among them.

That's right, friend. God says, “…they must not surrender the manslayer into his hand…” The text gives the reason: that man killed his neighbor accidentally without prior malice. So even if the avenger of blood pursues him, the answer is no.

It's actually true, friend. God says of the elders, “…they must not surrender the manslayer into his hand…” The avenger of blood can pursue him all the way there, and the man still isn't handed over. The text says he killed his neighbor accidentally without prior malice.

explanations.answer: Until his trial and the high priest's death
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. God says, “He is to stay in that city until he stands trial before the assembly and until the death of the high priest serving at that time.” That's two markers, and the text gives both. I'd love to tell you how many days that adds up to, but the verse doesn't say.

explanations.answer: Until the avenger of blood gives up
explanations.explanation: The text never says the avenger has to give up, friend. God says the man stays “…until he stands trial before the assembly and until the death of the high priest serving at that time.” That's the timeline. The avenger's mood doesn't set the clock.

explanations.answer: Until seven full years have passed
explanations.explanation: No number of years shows up in this verse, friend. God says the man stays until he stands trial before the assembly and until the death of the high priest serving at that time. Those are the two markers. I'd have loved a calendar date, but the text doesn't give one.

Yes, friend. God says, “Then the manslayer may return to his own home in the city from which he fled.” After the high priest serving at that time dies, home is open to him. I think that front door would look mighty good.

explanations.answer: To a different city of refuge
explanations.explanation: The text points him somewhere else, friend. After the high priest's death, God says, “Then the manslayer may return to his own home in the city from which he fled.” Another refuge city isn't what the verse names. Home is.

explanations.answer: Out to live in the wilderness
explanations.explanation: Nothing about the wilderness here, friend. God says, “Then the manslayer may return to his own home in the city from which he fled.” That's what the verse offers him after the death of the high priest serving at that time.

explanations.answer: Beyond the Jordan east of Jericho
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The text says, “And beyond the Jordan, east of Jericho, they designated Bezer…” Ramoth and Golan are over there too. So there are three cities on that side and three on the other.
Joppa doesn't come up in this passage, friend. The other three cities are “…beyond the Jordan, east of Jericho…” The first three were in the hill country. No coastline anywhere in these verses.

The Negev isn't mentioned here, friend. The text puts the other three cities “…beyond the Jordan, east of Jericho…” Bezer, Ramoth and Golan are the ones. Beersheba never makes the list in these verses.

explanations.answer: The Israelites and the foreigners among them
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The verse says, “These are the cities appointed for all the Israelites and foreigners among them…” Both are named, and the reason is “…so that anyone who kills a person unintentionally may flee there…” The unintentional part matters, and the verse keeps it right there.

explanations.answer: The Israelites but not the foreigners
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't leave the foreigners out, friend. It says the cities are “…appointed for all the Israelites and foreigners among them…” Both groups are named. Whoever kills a person unintentionally may flee there.

explanations.answer: The foreigners but not the Israelites
explanations.explanation: The Israelites are in there too, friend. The verse says, “These are the cities appointed for all the Israelites and foreigners among them…” It names both groups together. Neither one is left out.
